name: Sharjah
title: Sharjah UTM Services: Khor Fakkan, Hamriyah & Port Khalid
description: Sharjah thickness measurement at Khor Fakkan, Hamriyah and Port Khalid: ultrasonic renewal survey, pre-docking and hull structure gauging for ships.
h1: Ship Inspection in Sharjah: Thickness Gauging on Both Coasts
intro: Sharjah has ports on both coasts of the UAE. Khor Fakkan on the Gulf of Oman handles container transhipment outside the Strait of Hormuz, while Port Khalid and Hamriyah on the Gulf side serve general cargo, feeders, the oil and gas industry and marine fabrication. Superintendents with feeders, coasters, small tankers or offshore craft in the emirate can call on us for thickness measurement in Sharjah; the team comes from India and travels to whichever coast the ship is on.

highlights.p: Khor Fakkan faces the Gulf of Oman; Port Khalid and Hamriyah face the Gulf. A team already in the emirate can move between them by road when two ships' schedules line up.

Feeders, coasters and landing craft trading from Sharjah work warm water year-round with few long stops. Wastage builds steadily between surveys, so gauging at each renewal or sale carries real weight.

highlights.h: Yard work in Hamriyah Free Zone
highlights.p: Tugs, workboats and small offshore vessels come into the free zone's marine yards for repair. Gauging before blasting starts lets the repair list reflect measured wastage rather than visual estimates.

port.h: Sharjah's three ports and the traffic they handle
p: Sharjah's shipping divides between two coasts. Khor Fakkan, on the Gulf of Oman, is a deep-water container terminal whose position outside the Strait of Hormuz suits transhipment and feeder connections into the Gulf, and ships also wait and take bunkers off the east coast nearby. On the Gulf side, Port Khalid sits close to the city centre and handles containers, general cargo, ro-ro and project cargo, while Hamriyah Port to the north serves the Hamriyah Free Zone, with liquid and gas berths and an industrial waterfront of steel, fabrication and marine businesses.

Much of the tonnage here is regional. Feeder container ships shuttle between Khor Fakkan, Jebel Ali and the smaller Gulf ports; general cargo ships, coasters and landing craft trade around the Gulf and the Gulf of Oman and across to East Africa and the Indian subcontinent; small tankers and gas carriers serve the Hamriyah terminals. These ships rarely leave warm water and often work for years without a long lay-up, so wastage accumulates steadily between renewal surveys. When they do stop, it is usually for a docking at a Gulf yard or a few days at a repair berth, and that is the window for gauging. Landing craft deserve a separate note: their bow ramps, ramp hinges and flat bottoms take repeated beaching loads at unimproved landing sites, so they wear differently from conventional coasters.

That profile makes Sharjah demand distinctive. Many of the vessels are older and smaller, and are owned by regional operators who need gauging for class renewal surveys, for flag or charter requirements, or before sale to new owners. Hatch covers, coamings, holds and ballast tanks on general cargo ships and feeders take the brunt of the corrosion, and engine-room seawater systems on small ships run hard in warm, fouling water. Khor Fakkan adds an east-coast option for container ships and tankers that are already off the coast for bunkers or crew changes, without a detour through the strait.

facilities.h: Gauging at Khor Fakkan, Port Khalid and Hamriyah
p: Hull gauging in Hamriyah is usually tied to a repair or fabrication yard. Workboats, tugs, landing craft and small offshore vessels are slipped or lie alongside at the free zone's marine yards for repairs and surveys, and gauging is done before blasting and steel work start, so that the repair list reflects measured wastage rather than visual estimates. Small tankers and gas carriers serving the Hamriyah terminals are gauged at lay-by berths when idle between cargoes, with gas-freeing and entry permits arranged by the ship. Free-zone yards often handle several vessels at once, so the gauging schedule is agreed with the yard's planner to avoid clashing with blasting on a neighbouring hull.

At Port Khalid, gauging is done alongside on general cargo, ro-ro and container ships during longer calls, or on ships laid up waiting for employment. On the east coast, thickness gauging at Khor Fakkan is done on container ships alongside the terminal when the stay allows, and on tankers and bulk carriers waiting off the coast, reached by launch. Khor Fakkan is close to Fujairah, so a single mobilisation can cover ships at both, and the team can return to the Gulf-side ports by road the same day.
list: Khor Fakkan container terminal — piping, deck and hold gauging on container and feeder ships during longer stays at the east-coast berths
Off Khor Fakkan — pre-purchase and condition readings on tankers and bulkers lying off the east coast, reached by launch through the agent
Port Khalid — gauging on general cargo, ro-ro and project-cargo ships alongside, and on vessels laid up in the port awaiting employment
Hamriyah Free Zone marine yards — renewal-survey gauging of tugs, landing craft, workboats and small offshore vessels during repair periods
Hamriyah liquid and gas berths — condition gauging on small tankers and gas carriers when idle between cargoes, under the terminal's permit system

context.h: Regulation and market context for Sharjah ship owners
p: Sharjah's ports come under the UAE's port state control system as part of the Riyadh MoU, and older general cargo and feeder ships carry a higher risk profile under port state control targeting. Typical structural deficiencies on that tonnage are wasted deck and hatch-coaming plating, corroded air pipes and ventilators, and holed bulkheads. Gauging a known weak area ahead of time gives the owner both evidence and a repair plan before an inspector finds it. With no emission control area anywhere in the Gulf, ships here work to the 0.50% global sulphur limit, and scrubber-fitted container ships calling at Khor Fakkan need their wash-water piping watched.

Commercially, Sharjah sits within the UAE's ship-owning and trading community, with many regional operators, ship chandlers and repair contractors working across the emirates. Owners here often run mixed fleets of small ships that change hands frequently, and pre-purchase gauging is a practical protection for a buyer when the ship's maintenance record is thin. The climate adds to the case: humid summers, warm seawater and the dust and salt carried onto open decks shorten coating life on hatch covers and weather decks. Container feeder thickness gauging should therefore concentrate on hatch coamings, deck plating near the hatch corners and the tank top plating of the ballast tanks below.

jobs.p: Sharjah jobs are usually smaller in scope than a big-tanker docking but more varied: a feeder's renewal survey, a landing craft before sale, a tanker waiting off Khor Fakkan. Time on board is limited in nearly every case, so we plan readings by priority, prepare the TM plan from the ship's drawings, and agree access with the yard, terminal or master before the team boards.
list: Renewal-survey gauging of a general cargo ship laid up at Port Khalid: holds, hatch covers and coamings, tank tops, double-bottom ballast tanks and the weather deck.
Pre-docking readings on a container feeder taken alongside at Khor Fakkan, ahead of its second renewal survey at a Gulf yard after the next rotation.
Pre-purchase gauging of a landing craft at a Hamriyah yard, sampling the bow ramp structure, cargo deck and ballast tanks for a prospective buyer.
Seawater cooling and fire main pipe gauging on a small tanker idle at Hamriyah, where warm intake water and marine growth have thinned the pipe runs.
Condition gauging on a tanker waiting off Khor Fakkan for orders, covering deck, ballast tanks and accessible cargo-tank structure for an on-hire record.

logistics: Sharjah International Airport (SHJ) has direct flights from many Indian cities and is close to Port Khalid and Hamriyah; Dubai International (DXB) is an alternative. Khor Fakkan is reached by road through the mountains to the east coast. Port Khalid, Hamriyah and Khor Fakkan need ISPS passes arranged by the ship's agent, free-zone yards need entry permits through the yard, and for anchorage jobs the agent also books the launch. The team's UAE visas are processed before departure, so we ask for the ship's dates as early as they are known.

faqs.q: Can you cover a ship at Khor Fakkan and another at Port Khalid on one trip?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Both are in Sharjah and are linked by road through the mountains, so a team in the UAE for one job can move to the other coast if the dates line up. We plan the sequence around the ship with the firmer schedule and keep the agent at each port informed, so passes and launches are ready when the team arrives.

faqs.q: What usually needs gauging on an older general cargo ship in Sharjah?
faqs.a: General cargo ship gauging normally covers hatch coamings and covers, the weather deck around hatch corners, hold frames and brackets, tank tops and the double-bottom ballast tanks. On older ships, holds that have carried scrap, steel products or wet bulk cargo show local pitting and grooving at frame end brackets. The class renewal survey sets the minimum extent; for a buyer or charterer we widen it to the areas that drive repair decisions.

faqs.q: Is ship inspection in Sharjah possible on a vessel that is laid up?
faqs.a: Yes, and a lay-up is often the best moment. A ship idle at Port Khalid or a Hamriyah berth usually has gas-free tanks and time to spare, so a full TM plan can be worked through without cargo operations getting in the way. The owner must still arrange safe access, ventilation, lighting and a standby person for every tank entry, even with a reduced crew.

faqs.q: How does the east-coast location of Khor Fakkan help with planning?
faqs.a: Ships on the east coast are outside the Strait of Hormuz, so a container ship or tanker calling at Khor Fakkan or waiting nearby can be gauged without a detour into the Gulf. For owners whose vessels pass the east coast regularly, Khor Fakkan or nearby Fujairah can be the most convenient place to fit pre-docking readings or a condition check into the ship's normal trading pattern.
